America in Summary

What the formal presidential record says—and cannot say—across 1789–2026

1,057 speeches · 4.2M words · 45 presidents · 1789 - April 2026

SynthesisChange, continuity, and uncertaintyPost-story appendixExtreme speeches
Synthesis · Change, continuity, and uncertainty

What can presidential speech say about America in aggregate?

The chronology ends and six through-lines begin: agenda breadth, communication form, governing voice, adversaries, temporal appeal, and emotional register. Confirmatory, exploratory, and descriptive evidence remain visibly separate throughout. The present era is not uniquely doom-heavy; it is uniquely hype-heavy. Hype reaches 25.7 per 10,000 words versus 8.5 in the next-highest era, while doom is 8.9 versus a higher 9.3 in New Deal, world war & settlement.

America, in aggregate

The formal presidential record becomes more public-facing, more performed, less procedural, and more openly partisan. The category of enemy changes; presidents sell both tomorrow and yesterday; hope and doom move through the same historical shocks. These are changes in prepared presidential speech—not a single national personality.

Claim removed from the headline

Topic breadth expands early, then largely plateaus

Most of the visible topic-count increase occurs before the Civil War. Post-1860 movement is uneven and depends on the taxonomy and comparison baseline, so the Summary no longer presents a modern breadth surge or a topic-lifecycle heatmap as a central finding.

01 · Voice

Who is addressed changes. How the address is delivered changes.

Who: Congress gives way to the general public. How: written messages give way to spoken, broadcast, and other performed forms. The chart uses three mutually exclusive categories in each row so the transition reads at a glance.

∑ Measure · Assigned audience and delivery form · percent of era speeches

Definition. A mutually exclusive primary-form label used to describe this corpus's composition.

Unit. share of corpus speeches.

Calculation.

  1. Read the speech title and opening context
  2. Assign one declared medium label
  3. Count the labels within the displayed period

Example. A televised spoken address receives one primary label here, not both a spoken and broadcast count.

Limitation. It is not a complete inventory of delivery channels. Spoken addresses may also have been broadcast, and the label is an AI factual classification rather than archival metadata.

speeches with label / corpus speeches in period

02 · Conflict

The enemy changes category

The Summary now keeps every era on one categorical scale. It asks whether an adversarial mention names a nation, group, person, institution, or other target— without turning uncertain entity extraction into a parade of names.

∑ Measure · Share of adversarial entity mentions by entity category

Definition. The share of extracted adversarial entity mentions assigned to nation, group, person, institution, or other.

Unit. percent of adversarial mentions.

Calculation.

  1. Keep entity mentions with adversarial stance
  2. Assign the frozen entity type
  3. Count mentions by type within an era
  4. Divide by all adversarial entity mentions in that era

Example. If 60 of 100 adversarial entity mentions are nations, the nation category is 60%.

Limitation. Entity extraction and type labels can be wrong; the distribution excludes conflict wording without an extracted adversarial entity.

category adversarial mentions / all adversarial mentions

▤ Evidence · adversary_mix.parquet

Source artifact. combat/adversary_mix.parquet.

Statistical status. exploratory AI descriptive.

Denominator / support. All nine Story eras; categories sum to 100% within the adversarial entities extracted in each era.

Important caveat. Exploratory AI labels can misclassify entities and context. Category share describes the named targets, not all conflict language.

Definitions, downloads, and data-quality receipts →

Enemies are old; sustained partisan attack is newer

Annual messages contain enemy naming and zero-sum framing throughout the record. Partisan attack stays near the floor early and becomes a sustained feature later. The lines show observed paragraph shares only; confidence whiskers have been removed from this summary view.

∑ Measure · Enemy naming, zero-sum framing, and partisan attack · paragraph share

Definition. AI labels for enemy naming, zero-sum framing, partisan attack, and adversarial entity mentions.

Unit. percent of paragraphs.

Calculation.

  1. Join annotations on keyed paragraphs
  2. Canonicalize only declared aliases
  3. Count distinct supporting paragraphs
  4. Report rates and raw labels together

Example. China and Democrats can both appear in one era's ranked list when distinct paragraphs frame them adversarially.

Limitation. Context errors remain possible; a name in the list is not a judgment that it was a legitimate enemy.

flagged paragraphs / eligible paragraphs

03 · Time

Presidents sell both tomorrow and yesterday

Future language rises first and remains high. Nostalgia later catches up. Modern presidential speech can promise what comes next while recovering an imagined past; the two appeals are companions, not opposites.

∑ Measure · Future and nostalgia vocabulary per 10,000 words

Definition. Declared word families for forward-looking and backward-looking temporal appeal.

Unit. mentions per 10,000 words.

Calculation.

  1. Match declared word families
  2. Count all eligible words
  3. Scale each family to 10,000 words

Example. A speech can contain both families and therefore score highly on both.

Limitation. A match cannot establish whether a promise is feasible or a memory is accurate.

family count / words × 10,000

▤ Evidence · trends.parquet

Source artifact. register/trends.parquet.

Statistical status. descriptive.

Denominator / support. Annual-message/SOTU-only levels across the same nine fixed 30-year blocks.

Important caveat. Dictionary matches describe wording, not whether a future is feasible or a remembered past is accurate.

Definitions, downloads, and data-quality receipts →

What “nostalgia” means in the founding block

The dictionary contains only again, restore*, and back to. In 11 annual messages from 1789–1799 it finds 17 matches: 10 × again, 7 × restore*, and 0 × back to. The contexts are usually recurrence, restored order, or restored relations—not a golden-age appeal. That is a measurement warning, not evidence of founding-era nostalgia.

“America” overtakes “the United States” in the Progressive-era boundary

The naming crossover is another form of direct address: the institutional name gives way to the shorter national name in the centered series around 1910.

∑ Measure · National naming terms per 10,000 words

Definition. A count divided by all words and scaled to a same-sized 10,000-word container.

Unit. mentions per 10,000 words.

Calculation.

  1. Count included words
  2. Count all words
  3. Divide and multiply by 10,000

Example. Five mentions in 10,000 words equals 5 per 10,000.

Limitation. Words can carry different meanings in context.

count / words × 10,000

▤ Evidence · speech_markers.parquet

Source artifact. speech_markers.parquet.

Statistical status. descriptive.

Denominator / support. Centered five-year rolling sums of matches and all words.

Important caveat. The terms include adjectival and geographic uses and cannot prove national identity.

Definitions, downloads, and data-quality receipts →

Exactly what is counted. The America family matches the whole words America, American, and Americans; the comparison family matches the exact phrase United States. Each count is divided by all words and expressed per 10,000.

Why 1910 qualifies. The chart sums counts and words inside a centered five-year window. A sustained crossover requires five consecutive displayed windows in which the America family is higher. 1910 is the first start that passes; 1909 fails.

What it may suggest—and cannot prove. The pattern may suggest a shift toward a shorter public name for the nation. It cannot prove a change in national identity: the family also captures adjectival and geographic uses such as “American commerce” and “Central America,” the corpus mixes genres, and the Miller Center collection is not exhaustive.

04 · Emotional register

Hope divided by doom

This is Hope/Doom—not Hype/Doom. It reports broad NRC hope matches for each narrow doom-family match in supported centered five-year windows. The log scale keeps low and high ratios legible; event lines orient the timeline, and tooltips retain both rates.

∑ Measure · Aggregate NRC hope count divided by aggregate doom-family count

Definition. The aggregate NRC hope count divided by the aggregate doom-family count in a centered five-year window.

Unit. hope matches per doom match.

Calculation.

  1. Sum NRC hope, doom, and words within the window
  2. Require at least 20,000 words
  3. Suppress a zero doom denominator
  4. Divide aggregate counts

Example. A value of 80 means eighty NRC hope matches for each doom-family match in that window.

Limitation. The two dictionaries differ greatly in breadth. A ratio can rise when hope increases or doom falls, so absolute rates remain in tooltips.

Σ NRC hope matches / Σ doom matches

▤ Evidence · speech_markers.parquet

Source artifact. speech_markers.parquet.

Statistical status. descriptive.

Denominator / support. Centered five-year windows with at least 20,000 corpus words and a nonzero doom count.

Important caveat. Hope is a much broader dictionary than doom, so the ratio is not emotional balance or parity. Event lines do not identify causes.

05 · Audit

What America’s presidential record can—and cannot—say

Through-lineWhat changedWhat persisted What remains uncertain
AgendaTopic breadth expands mainly between the founding and Civil War eras, then largely plateaus.Money, war, rights, belonging, and national purpose repeatedly return under new vocabularies.Post-1860 breadth is baseline- and taxonomy-sensitive, so it is not a Summary headline.
CommunicationThe corpus moves from written messages toward broadcast performance and then an always-on environment.The annual message remains the closest repeated genre across the whole record.One assigned primary medium is not a complete inventory of channels, audiences, or platform activity.
Governing voiceLegal/procedural and hedged wording recedes while promotional and opponent-centered wording rises.Presidents still mix proposals, values, ceremony, administration, and persuasion.Vocabulary cannot measure competence, policy depth, persuasion, or sincerity.
ConflictThe mix of named enemy categories changes, while sustained partisan attack becomes more prominent later.Enemy naming and zero-sum frames occur in every era.Entity and paragraph labels cannot determine whether a target was legitimate or a frame sincere.
Time and emotionFuture and backward-looking terms can rise together; Hope/Doom varies around historical shocks.Presidents repeatedly promise renewal while describing danger.Dictionary matches are not intent; event markers orient time and do not identify causes.

Post-story appendix · Extreme speeches

Extreme speeches reveal extreme moments

Outlier cards belong after the history, where their word matches, percentiles, runner-ups, quotations, speech context, and metric definitions can be inspected without interrupting the chronology.

Open the extreme-speeches evidence cards

These rankings are a post-story interlude, not an era in the chronology. They compare speeches of at least 1,500 words so a short ceremonial statement cannot win on a handful of matches. Rates still require context: a dictionary cannot settle quotation, sarcasm, negation, or whether the president endorsed the matched words.

FearNRC fear + anger words, such as fear, danger, attack, destroy. Quotation and context can change their meaning.
HopeNRC trust + anticipation + joy words, such as hope, trust, peace, future.
BoostersDeclared intensifiers including never, always, certainly, absolutely, tremendous, incredible.
Us versus themThe literal pronouns they, them, themselves. This is a rough grammatical proxy—not proof of hostility or partisanship.
Superlativesgreatest, best, finest, strongest, worst, biggest, most important.

Illustrated AI labeling methodology, complete taxonomy, prompts, agreement audit, and limitations →

Method note: timelines are 5-year centered rolling rates weighted by word count, through April 2026. Points backed by under 20,000 words are not plotted - the corpus before ~1790 is a handful of speeches, and one personal inaugural should not set a national trend line. Dots are per president per year: 46 years have more than one president speaking, and the corpus files a few famous pre-presidency speeches (Nixon's Checkers speech, Reagan's "A Time for Choosing") under the later president. This is the formal register only - major prepared addresses; rallies, debates, and social media are outside the corpus, so every trend here is presidents at their most prepared.

Feedback and accuracy →
